paras: The attempted lynching of Joseph Ebright took place at Las Vegas, New Mexico, in March 1881, when railroad hands tried to lynch a saloon keeper who had shot and killed their friend, a Santa Fe railroad conductor. The sheriff got Ebright to jail, and he was later reported acquitted. The story spread nationally because a Philadelphia dispatch identified the dead man as James Currie, who had killed the actor Benjamin Porter in Texas, an identification other reports denied.

According to the Las Vegas Daily Optic, reprinted in Memphis, James H. Curry was a Southern-born railroad man of about forty who had worked as a yardmaster and for eight months as a freight conductor south of Las Vegas. The Optic described him as popular among the train crews and said his nearest relative was a daughter near Quincy, Illinois.

A Las Vegas special dated March 23 reported that Conductor J. H. Curry had been shot and instantly killed that morning by Joseph Ebright, a saloon keeper, and that the general impression was that the shooting was "uncalled for." The Philadelphia wire gave a different account: the dead man, on a drunken spree, had threatened several people, including a bartender, who shot him through the head in self-defense. A Santa Fe dispatch later said the quarrel began at a house of ill-fame and that the shooter was the keeper's husband.

After the shooting, "a party of railroad hands, friends of the dead man," attempted to lynch the bartender, according to the wire, but the sheriff got him to jail. The Las Vegas special described the danger more mildly, saying that "threats of lynching were freely indulged in." The local Gazette reported that Ebright would be kept safe in jail meanwhile and that a committee of citizens had been formed to aid the police and prevent mob violence, which it insisted was not a vigilance committee.

The Las Vegas Morning Gazette of March 25 said Ebright would have a preliminary examination on a charge of murdering Curry before Judge Steel. The wire instead reported that a coroner's jury had at once returned a verdict of self-defense, and a Santa Fe dispatch said the court acquitted Ebright on the evidence of himself and his wife, the only witnesses. Curry was buried from the Baptist chapel at Las Vegas, and the trainmaster held trains so that crews could attend the funeral.

No Black-press coverage is available for 1881, and the white press carried the story mainly as the fate of Porter's killer. From March 30 the Philadelphia wire ran from Pennsylvania to Nevada and Dakota under headlines such as "Retribution," "Righteous Retribution," "CURRIE A CORPSE" and "A Good Ridance." The Knoxville Chronicle, quoting the New York Evening Post, saw "special Providence" in the death and noted that, as in the Porter case, there had been an attempt to lynch the killer and a rescue by officers.

Corrections followed quickly: on March 31 the Chicago Tribune printed a Las Vegas report that the dead man was a freight conductor, and an April 1 Little Rock dispatch said he was a namesake with a violent past of his own. A Santa Fe dispatch carried by the National Republican on April 4 insisted that the dead man was Porter's killer after all. Neither the wire nor the corrections mentioned race, and the lynching attempt appeared in them only as a single sentence.

Reports disagree on the date, which local sources give as Wednesday, March 23, while the wire said March 24 and one copy March 25. They also differ on whether the shooting was self-defense, as the wire and the Santa Fe dispatch said, or "uncalled for," as the Las Vegas special reported, and on whether the crowd attempted a lynching or only threatened one.

bases: Railroad hands, friends of the man the saloon keeper shot, tried or threatened to lynch him and the sheriff kept him safe (A4, A22, A2); no one was killed by the crowd.

A 'party of railroad hands' tried or threatened to lynch Ebright for killing their friend, but the sheriff got him away and no one was killed (A4, A22); this is an attempted lynching, and the coverage names no Black person in it.

A Las Vegas special (A1, A22), the local Gazette (A2) and the Philadelphia wire (A4) independently report the saloon shooting and the danger of mob violence against the shooter, though they disagree on the date, the dead man's identity and the legal outcome.

accounts.label: Philadelphia wire (private message to Marshal Kerns)
accounts.gist: James Currie, killer of Porter, on a drunken spree threatened a bartender, who shot him in self-defense; railroad hands attempted to lynch the bartender, the sheriff got him to jail, and a coroner's jury found self-defense.

accounts.label: Santa Fe dispatch
accounts.gist: The dead man was Porter's killer after all; drunk, he quarreled at a house of ill-fame and was shot by the keeper's husband, whom the court acquitted on the couple's own evidence.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Philadelphia wire under headlines treating the death as justice for Porter's killer: 'Retribution', 'Righteous Retribution', 'A Good Ridance', 'CURRIE A CORPSE'.
Western specials and the local press reported the dead man as a railroad conductor and the shooting as 'uncalled for', with no Porter link.
The Knoxville Chronicle, quoting the Evening Post, called the death a case of 'special Providence' and noted the parallel attempt to lynch and rescue by officers.

conflicts.note: The Las Vegas special datelined March 23, the Optic of March 23 and the local Gazette agree on March 23; they are closer to the event than the Philadelphia wire.
